name: Derby shoes

image.caption: Tricker's Robert derby shoes in brown suede

lead: A derby is a lace-up shoe or boot with the lace tabs (eyestays) stitched on top of the vamp, called open lacing. It is a staple of men's smart-casual and business dress and is often contrasted with the closed-lacing Oxford.

It helps looks through style: a clean leather derby polishes an outfit, and the open lacing accommodates higher insteps and wider feet more easily than Oxfords. Wikipedia notes the style began as sporting and hunting footwear in the 1850s and became town wear by the early 1900s.

paras: Worn with chinos, jeans, suits or tailored trousers in leather or suede, in colours such as black, brown or tan. Buckskin "white bucks" are a traditional Ivy League look.
No particular risks; fit and break-in blisters are the usual practical concerns. Derbies are generally seen as less formal than Oxfords for the most formal occasions.

angle.text: A derby gives a finished, dressed-up look at the feet while its open lacing is a little easier to fit around the instep than an Oxford. It slots into smart-casual and business wardrobes.

lead: A derby is a shoe or boot with large quarters and lacing tabs stitched on top of the vamp, a construction called open lacing; it is also known as a gibson.[1] The Oxford, by contrast, has its tabs stitched underneath the vamp (closed lacing).[1]

Wikipedia reports the derby became a popular sporting and hunting boot in the 1850s and was considered suitable for town wear by the early 1900s.[1] In American usage it is sometimes called a blucher, although strictly a blucher has quarter and vamp cut from one piece.[1]
People use derbies to add polish to everyday and business outfits. Light suede or nubuck versions called "white bucks", often with red soles, became associated with Ivy League style.[1]

paras: The defining feature is the pair of eyestays sewn on top of the vamp, which lets the throat of the shoe open wider.[1] Buckskin versions are called "bucks", and light suede or nubuck ones were especially common.[1]

The style rose as sport and hunting footwear in the 1850s and reached town wear by the early 1900s.[1] The term "white-shoe firm" for elite law firms is linked to Ivy League fashion that favoured white bucks.[1]

timeline.event: Derby becomes a popular sporting and hunting boot.[1]
